questions.prompt: What is the median of a dataset?
options: The total divided by the count
questions.explanation: Sort the data, then take the middle value — the median.
questions.misconception: Total ÷ count is the mean, and the most frequent is the mode — the median is the middle after sorting.

questions.prompt: What is the first step to find a median?
options: Sort the data from low to high
questions.explanation: You must order the data before the middle makes sense.
questions.misconception: The mean adds; the median orders — without sorting, 'middle' is meaningless.

questions.explanation: Sorted already: 1, 3, 9, 12, 20 — the middle (3rd) value is 9.
questions.misconception: The median is the middle position, not the middle value of the range — 9 is the 3rd item, not 10.

questions.explanation: Even count — average the two middle values: (5 + 8) ÷ 2 = 6.5.
questions.misconception: There is no single middle item with 4 values, so you average the two middle ones instead of picking either.

questions.prompt: Why does a giant outlier barely affect the median?
options: The median depends on position, not the outlier's size
The median adds all values first
questions.explanation: Only the middle position matters — a huge value just sits at the far end.
questions.misconception: The mean adds every value, so it feels outliers — the median counts only positions.
